client: I've been really struggling at my new marketing job lately. I'm constantly comparing myself to my coworkers who seem to know exactly what they're doing, while I'm barely keeping up with all the tight deadlines. Part of me wonders if therapy can even help with this - it's not like you can magically make me better at my job, right?
therapist: "It sounds like you're feeling overwhelmed and stuck in this cycle of comparison, especially with the pressure of deadlines. Therapy won't magically make you better at your job, but it can help you explore those thoughts and find ways to shift your perspective. What evidence do you have that you're 'barely keeping up,' or could there be another way to look at it?"

client:
I know logically that I'm meeting my deadlines, but it still feels like I'm barely scraping by while everyone else is thriving. When I see my coworkers getting praised or promoted, it just reinforces that voice in my head saying I'm not good enough. 

The evidence thing is hard because my brain just dismisses any positive examples - like if I point out that I did finish a project on time, I immediately think "but it could've been better" or "others did more."
therapist: "I hear how that critical voice quickly dismisses any evidence of your successes - that must feel exhausting to constantly battle against. It might help to notice that pattern where accomplishments get minimized ('but it could've been better') as it happens. What do you think keeps that voice so persistent, even when facts suggest you're meeting expectations?"

client: I don't know why that voice is so persistent - maybe because I grew up with parents who were never satisfied no matter what I did. Even when I can logically see I've done well, it's like my brain automatically looks for flaws. It's exhausting, but trying to ignore it feels like I'm just lying to myself.
therapist: "It makes sense that this critical voice feels so ingrained when it echoes those early experiences with your parents - that kind of conditioning runs deep. You're describing something important: the struggle between knowing your worth logically, yet feeling like acknowledging it would be dishonest - can we explore that tension a bit more?"

client:
It's just...even when I try to acknowledge my worth, it feels like I'm lying to myself. Like I'm pretending to be someone better than I actually am. And part of me worries that if I stop being so hard on myself, I'll become lazy or complacent. 

That tension you mentioned is really uncomfortable because on one hand I want to feel better, but on the other hand being self-critical has always felt like the "right" way to be.
therapist: "It sounds like that self-critical voice has served as a kind of motivator for you, even though it comes with so much pain. Let's gently challenge that idea - what if being kinder to yourself could actually help you perform better, rather than making you complacent? What might that look like in your daily work?"

client:
I get what you're saying, but I'm not sure I believe being kinder to myself would actually help. When I try to go easy on myself, I just feel like I'm making excuses for not being good enough. The self-criticism at least keeps me pushing forward, even if it hurts. 

It's hard to imagine being gentle with myself when I make mistakes at work - that just sounds like letting myself off the hook. What if I become lazy or stop trying as hard? I've always believed the pressure is what makes me perform.
therapist: "I hear how deeply you believe that self-criticism is necessary for your performance - that belief feels very protective, even as it causes you pain. Let's experiment with this: what if we viewed self-compassion not as 'letting yourself off the hook,' but as giving yourself the same constructive feedback you'd give a valued colleague who made a mistake?"

client:
I get what you're saying, but it's hard to imagine being that gentle with myself. When my colleague messes up, I can see their potential, but with myself all I see are the flaws. It feels like if I stop being hard on myself, I'll just become lazy and make even more mistakes. 

The comparison to a colleague makes sense logically, but emotionally it's completely different - like there's this voice in my head that says "they deserve kindness, but you don't."
therapist: "That double standard you're describing - kindness for others but not for yourself - sounds like it's creating a lot of emotional exhaustion. Let's gently explore where that belief that 'you don't deserve kindness' might come from - when did you first start feeling that way about yourself?"

client: I think it started when I was a kid - my parents were always stressed about money, and I felt like I had to be the "easy" child who didn't cause trouble. But even now as an adult, that feeling stuck with me. It's hard to imagine being kind to myself when I still feel like I'm just creating burdens for people.
therapist: "It sounds like that childhood role of being the 'easy child' became more than just behavior - it shaped how you see your worth as a person. That burden of feeling like you must never inconvenience others seems to still weigh heavily on you now. What would it feel like to challenge that belief that your needs are a burden to others?"

client:
I don't know... the idea of putting my needs first makes me really uncomfortable. Even now, I can hear my mom's voice saying "don't be difficult" whenever I think about asking for help. It's like I've spent my whole life proving I'm not a burden, and now that feels like part of who I am. 

But at the same time, I'm exhausted from always putting others first. I just don't know how to change without feeling selfish or guilty.
therapist: "That exhaustion you're describing makes so much sense - you've been carrying this belief about being a burden for so long, and it's clearly weighing you down. Let's go slowly here: what would it look like to take one small step toward prioritizing your needs, without it feeling like you're betraying who you are?"

client:
I don't know... even the idea of prioritizing myself makes me feel selfish. Like if I start doing that, people will think I don't care about them anymore. It's scary because being helpful is such a big part of how I see myself. 

But I am so tired all the time. Maybe I could try something small, but I'm worried I'll either do too much and burn out, or do too little and feel guilty. It feels like there's no right answer.
therapist: "I hear how deeply this fear of being seen as selfish is holding you back, even as you recognize the toll it's taking on you. That middle ground between burnout and guilt feels impossible to find right now. What would be one tiny way you could practice self-care this week that wouldn't trigger those fears of abandoning others?"

client: I know I should try something small, but even the idea of taking time for myself makes me feel guilty. What if people think I'm being lazy or uncaring? Maybe I could try reading for 15 minutes before bed, but I keep thinking about all the things I should be doing instead.
therapist: "I notice how quickly your mind jumps to 'shoulds' when you consider taking even 15 minutes for yourself - that guilt seems to appear instantly. Let's observe that reaction together: what do you think it says about your beliefs regarding rest and self-care?"
